lines.text: Standing stones, Roman walls, Viking raiders, kings and queens, factories and empire. This is the long story of the United Kingdom, from Stonehenge to today.
About five thousand years ago, farmers on Salisbury Plain began raising a ring of huge stones, lined up with the midsummer sunrise. Why, we still argue.
Rome came and stayed for centuries. Around the year 122, the emperor Hadrian ordered a stone wall across the north, marking the edge of his empire.
After Rome, the English kingdoms faced the Vikings. Alfred of Wessex held them back when others fell, and he built a navy and championed learning in English.
His grandson Athelstan went further. After taking York in 927, he became the first king to rule the whole of England.
Yet the Danes returned. In 1016 Cnut took the English crown, and soon ruled Denmark and Norway too, a North Sea empire governed by English law.
Edward the Confessor rebuilt Westminster Abbey. When he died without an heir in January 1066, the fight for the crown began.
Harold Godwinson took the throne. He would be the last Anglo-Saxon king, reigning just nine months.
Across the Channel, William, Duke of Normandy, had his own claim, and he was ready to fight for it.
His son William Rufus would rule after him, until an arrow killed him while hunting in the New Forest.
To hold London, William began a great castle by the Thames. The Tower of London has since been palace, prison and mint, and still guards the Crown Jewels.
In October 1066, near Hastings, William defeated Harold. The Norman conquest remade English law, language, land and nobility.
William's youngest son, Henry, seized the throne when his brother died, and ruled for thirty-five years.
William wanted to know exactly what his kingdom held. The great survey that followed was so final that people named it after the Day of Judgement.
After Henry, his nephew Stephen and his daughter Matilda fought over the crown, a civil war remembered as the Anarchy.
Henry the Second brought order back and ruled from England deep into France. He grew the royal courts and the common law, and clashed with Thomas Becket.
His son Richard the Lionheart spent little time at home. He led the Third Crusade, made a truce with Saladin, and died fighting in France.
His brother John lost Normandy, and his angry barons forced him to make promises he never wished to keep.
John's son Henry the Third became king at nine and reigned fifty-six years, rebuilding Westminster Abbey and facing a barons' revolt.
Those promises were Magna Carta, sealed at Runnymede in 1215. It said even the king was bound by law, and it became a lasting symbol of freedom.
Edward the First, called Longshanks, conquered Wales, fought for years in Scotland, and called parliaments that included commoners.
His son lost to Robert the Bruce at Bannockburn, and was forced from the throne in favour of his own son.
Edward the Third ruled for fifty years. He claimed the crown of France, and so began the Hundred Years' War.
Then came the plague. The Black Death swept in from Asia and killed a huge share of the people, changing work, wages and faith.
Richard the Second faced the Peasants' Revolt at just fourteen. Years later his cousin Henry Bolingbroke took his crown.
As Henry the Fourth, Bolingbroke became the first king of the House of Lancaster, and spent his reign putting down revolts.
His son Henry the Fifth renewed the war with France and was named heir to the French throne, but died young before he could claim it.
His great victory came in 1415 at Agincourt, where tired English longbowmen, helped by deep mud, beat a far larger French army.
Henry the Sixth became king as a baby. He lost the lands in France, and the rivalries around his weak rule turned to war.
Edward the Fourth, of York, won the throne in battle, lost it for a few months, then ruled until his death.
His brother Richard the Third took the crown from his young nephew. He died at Bosworth, and his bones were found under a car park in Leicester in 2012.
These were the Wars of the Roses, decades of fighting between Lancaster and York for the English throne.
They ended with Henry Tudor, who won at Bosworth in 1485, married Elizabeth of York, and joined the two rival houses.
Before him, the boy king Edward the Fifth and his brother had vanished in the Tower, the Princes in the Tower, never seen again.
Henry the Eighth married six times. When the Pope would not end his first marriage, he broke with Rome and closed the monasteries.
His daughter Mary became the first queen to rule England in her own right. She brought back the Catholic faith and burned hundreds of Protestants.
Her sister Elizabeth reigned for forty-four years, saw off the Spanish Armada, and presided over a golden age of voyages and theatre.
Henry's break had created the Church of England, free of the Pope, and in time the mother church of Anglicans worldwide.
His son Edward the Sixth became king at nine. His advisers pushed the church toward Protestant ways, with a new prayer book in English.
When Edward died, his teenage cousin Lady Jane Grey was proclaimed queen. She lasted about nine days, and was later executed.
In Elizabeth's age, a glover's son from Stratford wrote Hamlet, Macbeth and Romeo and Juliet. Shakespeare's words still shape the English language.
In 1603 James, King of Scotland, became King of England too, joining the two crowns, and gave his name to a famous Bible.
Meanwhile English ships were claiming lands overseas. In time the British Empire would become the largest in history, spreading English across the world.
Oliver Cromwell, a member of Parliament and a soldier, led the army against the king, and later ruled as Lord Protector.
Charles the First believed kings ruled by divine right. He clashed with Parliament, lost a civil war, and was beheaded.
In 1660 his son Charles the Second was restored. His reign saw the Great Fire of London, the Royal Society, and theatres reopened.
His Catholic brother James the Second would not last. He lost his throne in 1688 and was beaten in Ireland at the Boyne.
The Civil War between king and Parliament tore the country apart, and for over a decade England had no monarch at all.
In this restless century, Isaac Newton set out the laws of motion and gravity, invented calculus, and split white light into colours.
The Dutch prince William of Orange was invited to take the crown, and accepted a Bill of Rights that limited royal power.
Later, in 1714, the crown passed to George of Hanover. In his reign Robert Walpole became the first prime minister.
William ruled alongside his wife Mary the Second, a Protestant daughter of James, who governed alone while he was at war.
Queen Anne was the last of the Stuarts. In her reign, the Acts of Union of 1707 joined England and Scotland as Great Britain.
George the Second was the last British king to lead his troops into battle, at Dettingen in 1743.
That change of 1688 was the Glorious Revolution, when Parliament and William of Orange pushed James aside with little bloodshed in England.
The Bill of Rights followed: no taxes without Parliament, free speech in its debates, and no cruel punishments.
And with the union of 1707, a new state was born. Ireland would join in 1801, and most of it leave again in 1922.
Captain James Cook sailed three times into the Pacific, mapping New Zealand and eastern Australia, before he was killed at Hawaii.
At home, James Watt made the steam engine far more efficient. His engines drove the mines and mills, and the unit of power bears his name.
George the Third reigned almost sixty years, through the loss of America and the long wars with Napoleon.
Around him, Britain was changing faster than anywhere on Earth. The Industrial Revolution brought steam, railways, factories and swelling cities.
While his father was ill, George the Fourth ruled as Prince Regent, and is remembered for lavish buildings like the Royal Pavilion at Brighton.
His brother William, the Sailor King, saw the Reform Act of 1832 change who could vote.
In quiet country rooms, Jane Austen wrote Pride and Prejudice and Emma, sharp and funny tales of marriage, money and manners.
At sea, in 1805, Nelson's fleet destroyed the French and Spanish off Trafalgar. Nelson died, but Britain ruled the waves.
Charles Darwin sailed on the Beagle, and decades later published his theory of evolution by natural selection, changing how we see life itself.
Charles Dickens wrote Oliver Twist and A Christmas Carol, stories that laid bare the poverty of Victorian Britain.
In 1815, at Waterloo, Wellington and the Prussians defeated Napoleon for the last time.
Queen Victoria reigned for over sixty-three years, Empress of India, at the heart of a vast empire, and an age took her name.
Florence Nightingale nursed soldiers in the Crimean War, used numbers to prove that dirt was killing them, and made nursing a profession.
In 1833 Britain ended slavery across most of its empire. The owners were paid handsomely; the freed people received nothing.
Victoria's son Edward waited almost sixty years to be king, and gave his name to the Edwardian era.
In 1851 London showed off to the world, with machines and goods from many lands inside a vast glass hall, the Crystal Palace.
A dozen years later, the world's first underground railway opened beneath London's streets.
George the Fifth led the country through the First World War, and in 1917 changed the royal family's name to Windsor.
Winston Churchill, soldier, writer and politician, would lead Britain through its darkest hour with words that still echo.
Edward the Eighth was king for less than a year. In 1936 he gave up the throne to marry Wallis Simpson.
His shy brother became George the Sixth, and stayed in London through the Blitz.
Alan Turing imagined the machine that defines what computers can do, and in the war helped break the German Enigma codes at Bletchley Park.
The First World War cost Britain a generation of young men. Millions died, empires fell, and the map of the world was redrawn.
In 1922 the BBC began broadcasting, a public voice for the nation, paid for by a licence fee.
Margaret Thatcher became the first woman prime minister. She sold off state industries, curbed the unions, and won the Falklands War.
Elizabeth the Second came to the throne in 1952 and reigned for over seventy years, longer than any British monarch before her.
Back in the summer of 1940, the Royal Air Force fought the Luftwaffe over southern England, and Hitler's invasion was put off.
Then came the Blitz. For months, bombs fell on British cities, killing tens of thousands, but Britain would not make peace.
Stephen Hawking studied black holes and the birth of the universe, and his Brief History of Time brought the cosmos to millions.
After the war, in 1948, came the National Health Service, free to everyone at the point of use.
That same year, a prince was born who would wait over sixty years as heir, Charles, known for his work on charities and the environment.
Tim Berners-Lee, working at CERN in 1989, proposed the World Wide Web, and wrote the first browser and server.
In the sixties four young men from Liverpool, the Beatles, changed pop and rock music forever.
Keir Starmer, a lawyer, led Labour to a landslide in 2024 and became prime minister, before stepping down in July 2026.
Before him, Boris Johnson, once mayor of London, became prime minister and took the country out of the European Union.
J. K. Rowling's Harry Potter books sold hundreds of millions of copies and enchanted a generation of readers.
Andy Burnham, the mayor of Greater Manchester, returned to Parliament in 2026 and followed Starmer as prime minister.
In 1982 Argentina seized the Falkland Islands, and within a few months British forces had taken them back.
In 1994 the Channel Tunnel opened, joining Britain to the continent for the first time since the Ice Age.
In 1998 the Good Friday Agreement brought shared government to Northern Ireland and largely ended the Troubles.
On a July morning in 2005, suicide bombers struck three Underground trains and a bus in London, killing fifty-two people.
Seven years later, London became the first city to host the Summer Olympics three times.
In 2014 Scotland voted on leaving the United Kingdom. About fifty-five percent chose to stay.
Two years later, Britain voted to leave the European Union, and in January 2020 it left.
In 2017 fire raced up the cladding of Grenfell Tower in London, killing seventy-two people.
Then the pandemic came. Lockdowns emptied the streets, and vaccines arrived at record speed.
In September 2022, after seventy years on the throne, Queen Elizabeth died, and the nation said goodbye.
From standing stones to a new king, the story of these islands is still being written.
